name: Photochromic (transition) lenses

lead: Photochromic lenses are glasses lenses that change tint when exposed to ultraviolet light. Indoors they are clear or lightly tinted; outdoors they darken and act like sunglasses.

For appearance, this lets people who wear prescription glasses keep an eye-visible, clear look indoors and avoid squinting outdoors, without carrying a second pair. Silver-halide chemistry in glass and organic molecules in plastic lenses drive the change.

paras: People order them as an option on prescription or non-prescription lenses, in a range of tint colours such as grey or brown. They darken within a minute of sun exposure and take several minutes to clear. Many pair them with frames chosen for face shape.

Heat reduces how dark they get and cold slows clearing, so they may not reach full sunglass darkness in very hot weather. Because they respond to UV, they typically stay lighter behind car windshields that block UV. These are performance characteristics, not safety hazards.

web.title: Effect of a Photochromic Contact Lens on Visual Function Indoors (RCT)
Photochromic Contact Lenses in Indoor and Outdoor Conditions

chain: Works as sunglasses outdoors and clear glasses indoors
One pair serves both looks and eyes stay visible indoors
angle.text: Wearers get a sunglasses look outdoors and visible eyes indoors from the same frames, and a lens that reduces squinting in bright light.

lead: Photochromic lenses, often sold under the Transitions brand name, are eyeglass lenses that darken when exposed to ultraviolet light and return to clear or lightly tinted in shade [1]. They give wearers of prescription glasses a single pair that works indoors and outdoors, so the eyes stay visible to other people inside and the glasses double as sunglasses outside.

For appearance, the appeal is a sunglasses look and a normal-glasses look from the same frames, with less squinting in bright light. Wearers choose them as a convenience and a style option, and tint colours such as grey and brown are offered so the darkened state suits the wearer's taste.

The technology was developed at Corning Glass Works in the early 1960s by William Armistead and S. Donald Stookey, who reported silver-halide photochromic glass in the journal Science in 1964 [1]. Silver-based glass lenses were later largely replaced by plastic lenses using organic molecules such as oxazines and naphthopyrans [1]. Transitions Optical, a joint venture formed in 1990, became the best-known brand [2]. Published human research on photochromic lenses has focused on glare, light discomfort and contrast, mostly with photochromic contact lenses [3][4].
infobox: William H. Armistead and S. Donald Stookey [1]
Substantially under a minute, deepening for about 15 minutes [1]
Noticeably lighter in 2 minutes; about 15 minutes to full clear [1]

paras: A photochromic lens is an optical lens that darkens in response to high-frequency light, most commonly ultraviolet radiation, and reverts to its clear state when that light is removed [1]. Glass versions respond to UV-A light, while plastic versions respond to UV and generally not to ordinary indoor artificial light, which is why they stay clear in a room [1].

Lenses are sold as prescription or plain-glass options and appear in everyday eyewear as well as sport sunglasses and ski goggles. The Wikipedia entry lists makers such as INVU, Tifosi, Oakley, ZEISS, Serengeti Eyewear and Persol as offering photochromic-tinted sunglass lenses [1].

In glass lenses, microcrystals of silver halide, usually silver chloride, are embedded in the glass. UV-A light between about 320 and 400 nm drives electrons from the glass onto silver ions, forming visible elemental silver that darkens the lens; in shade the reaction reverses [1]. Because the effect depends on glass thickness, variable-thickness prescription lenses were a difficulty for glass [1].

In plastic lenses, usually polycarbonate or similar materials, organic photochromic molecules such as oxazines and naphthopyrans change structure under UV and absorb a substantial share of visible light. The molecules are set in a surface layer of uniform thickness up to about 150 micrometres [1].

Reversal is a thermal process. Reference descriptions state that higher temperatures make lenses less dark, which can prevent full sunglass darkness in very hot weather, while cold lenses darken more but clear more slowly [1].

Plastic lenses are described as darkening substantially in under a minute and continuing to deepen for roughly 15 minutes. On removal of UV they are noticeably lighter within about 2 minutes, mostly clear within about 5, and fully clear in about 15 [1]. A report from University College London's Institute of Ophthalmology, cited by Wikipedia, found that at their clearest the lenses can still absorb up to 20 percent of ambient light [1].

Because window glass in cars filters much of the UV that activates plastic photochromics, these lenses often darken less inside a vehicle. A Grokipedia overview, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes the XTRActive line as designed for extra darkness including in vehicles, and lists typical darkened transmission and slower cold-weather clearing [5]. Manufacturers of specialty lines market versions intended to respond to a wider range of light.

Photochromic glass was developed by William H. Armistead and S. Donald Stookey at Corning Glass Works. Their paper, "Photochromic Silicate Glasses Sensitized by Silver Halides," appeared in Science on 10 April 1964 [1]. Grokipedia dates the associated US patent to 1965 and associates early Corning production with the Photogray name [5].

Plastic lenses with organic photochromic compounds later became the dominant form [1]. Transitions Optical was founded in 1990 as a joint venture between PPG Industries (51 percent) and Essilor (49 percent); in April 2014 Essilor acquired PPG's stake, and the company is now part of EssilorLuxottica [2]. Between 2009 and 2012 Transitions was title sponsor of a PGA Tour golf event in Florida and has sponsored professional cycling [2].

Other optical makers, among them Hoya, also entered the market [5]. Grokipedia reports that photochromic lenses reached more than 11 percent of global eyeglass-lens sales in the early 2020s, a figure it does not tie to a stated survey [5].

People who wear glasses full-time choose photochromic lenses to avoid carrying separate sunglasses or clip-ons. Indoors the lens looks like clear glass, so eye contact and facial expression stay visible, and outdoors the same frames present as sunglasses. Choice of frames, tint colour (grey and brown are common) and coatings lets wearers match the darkened look to their style.

Some wearers also pair photochromics with frames chosen to suit face shape, treating the darkened state as part of how the glasses look outdoors. Because plastic photochromics respond to UV rather than to visible light alone, wearers describe the tint as varying with weather, season and shade, which some regard as part of the lens's character.
No studies found on photochromic lenses as an appearance aid. Human studies of photochromic lenses examine visual function, chiefly in contact lenses.

A 2020 randomized, subject-masked contralateral trial in Optometry and Vision Science enrolled 62 adults (60 completed) and compared a photochromic contact lens in one eye with a non-photochromic control in the other, tested in the lens's minimally activated indoor-like state. The photochromic eye tolerated more glare before losing sight of a target, squinted less in response to bright light, recovered vision faster after a bright flash (about 8.8 versus 17.3 seconds) and had better chromatic contrast thresholds. The study was funded by the lens manufacturer, Johnson & Johnson Vision Care [3].

A 2023 pilot simulation study in the Journal of Clinical Medicine used spectacle lenses mimicking photochromic contact-lens transmittance in 33 healthy university students. Outdoors in sunlight, the activated condition gave better contrast sensitivity than no lens or a non-activated lens; indoors and under glare, differences were not significant, and visual acuity did not differ. The authors noted the small, young sample and that the simulation did not fully replicate real contact-lens wear [4].

timeline.event: Armistead and Stookey develop silver-halide photochromic glass at Corning Glass Works [1].
Armistead and Stookey publish "Photochromic Silicate Glasses Sensitized by Silver Halides" in Science (10 April) [1].
A US patent for the glass is issued to Armistead and Stookey, according to Grokipedia [5].
Transitions Optical is founded as a joint venture of PPG Industries and Essilor [2].
Transitions becomes title sponsor of a PGA Tour event in Florida, running through 2012 [2].
Essilor acquires PPG's stake, making Transitions a wholly owned subsidiary [2].
Randomized trial of a photochromic contact lens reports less glare disability and faster photostress recovery [3].
Pilot study reports better outdoor contrast sensitivity with activated photochromic lenses [4].
